wallacea-crossers.name: The first crossers of Wallacea
wallacea-crossers.bio: Hominins who crossed the sea from Bali or Java into the islands east of the Wallace Line between about a million and 700,000 years ago, and reached Flores, where their fossils lie at Mata Menge. They were probably descended from Homo erectus, grown small on the island, and probably ancestral to Homo floresiensis. Whether they crossed on purpose, on rafts, or were carried off by storms and floods, nobody knows.

sahul-first-peoples.name: The first peoples of Sahul
sahul-first-peoples.bio: The ancestors of Aboriginal Australians and of the first peoples of New Guinea, who crossed from the islands of Wallacea to Sahul, the one continent of Australia and New Guinea, between about 65,000 and 50,000 years ago. The sea stood more than 100 metres lower than today, and still every way across meant open water.

pesse-canoe-makers.name: The makers of the Pesse canoe
pesse-canoe-makers.bio: Mesolithic people of the north European plain who, between about 8040 and 7510 BC, hollowed a Scots pine log into the oldest boat yet found. Nothing else of theirs is known from the find; the canoe stands for them.

leif-erikson.name: Leif Erikson
leif-erikson.bio: The son of Erik the Red, he grew up in the Norse settlement his father founded in Greenland. The Icelandic sagas have him reach Vinland, usually read as the coast of North America, about half a millennium before Columbus; the Norse site at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland may be his. After his father died he led the Greenland settlement.

images.author: Christian Krohg
images.note: No likeness survives; a Norwegian painting of nine centuries later.

born.label: Leif Erikson born in Iceland, c. 970s
born.text: The sagas do not say where. Iceland, where his parents met, is the likeliest country, and Haukadalur, his mother's family's valley, the usual guess; the mark stands at Eiríksstaðir, the farm there.

death.label: Leif Erikson died, c. 1020, probably at Brattahlíð
death.text: The sagas are silent. He is last named alive about 1018–19 and his son Thorkell held the chieftaincy by 1025; Brattahlíð, the family estate, is the likeliest place.
death.source: Leif Erikson (Wikipedia): no saga records his death

marco-polo.name: Marco Polo
marco-polo.bio: A Venetian merchant who set out with his father Niccolò and uncle Maffeo in 1271 and reached the court of Kublai Khan, who sent him on missions across the empire and beyond. He was back in Venice in 1295. His Travels, written down about 1300, gave Europe its first broad look at China, Persia and India.

images.author: Maître de la mazarine et collab.
Unknown
images.note: A woodcut on the first German edition of his book, a century and a half after his death.

born.label: Marco Polo born at Venice, c. 1254
born.text: Born about 1254 in Venice; no document of the time records the day.
born.doubt: Korčula, an island off the Dalmatian coast, says he was born there and shows visitors a house it calls his; others have put his birth in Constantinople.

death.label: Marco Polo died at Venice, 8 Jan 1324
death.text: He died at home in January 1324. His will freed Peter, his Tatar slave. Priests are said to have urged him on his deathbed to take back his Book; he answered that he had not told the half of what he saw.

ibn-battuta.name: Ibn Battuta
ibn-battuta.bio: A scholar and judge from Tangier who spent about thirty years, 1325 to 1354, travelling through much of Africa, Asia and Iberia, by most counts farther than any other traveller before modern times. Near the end of his life he dictated the account known as the Rihla.

images.author: Ibn Juzayy; Bibliothèque nationale de France
Léon Benett
images.note: No likeness survives; an illustration for Jules Verne's Découverte de la terre, five centuries after his death.

born.label: Ibn Battuta born at Tangier, 24 Feb 1304
born.text: The day comes from his own account in the Rihla.

death.label: Ibn Battuta died in Morocco, c. 1369
death.text: He dictated the Rihla at Fez in 1355–56 and died in Morocco about 1368–69. Nobody recorded where, so the skull stands in the country, not on a town.

alternatives.label: Died at Marrakesh, by one modern account
alternatives.text: Some modern summaries put his death at Marrakesh; the Rihla ends in 1355 and no chronicle of his death survives. The tomb shown at Tangier, his birthplace, is unproven: it marks a burial tradition, not a place of death.
alternatives.source: Wikipedia, Ibn Battuta (infobox); the Tangier tomb is captioned "purported"

zheng-he.name: Zheng He
zheng-he.bio: Born Ma He to a Hui Muslim family in Yunnan, he served the Yongle Emperor, who gave him the name Zheng. Between 1405 and 1433 he commanded seven treasure voyages across the Indian Ocean as far as the Swahili coast, and he served as commander of the southern capital, Nanjing.

images.author: Mao Yuanyi, Wubei Zhi, and an unknown cartographer
Unknown
images.note: Published about 1600 in a fictionalised account of his voyages.

born.label: Zheng He born in Yunnan, 1371
born.text: Born Ma He to a Hui family of Kunyang, Kunming, then held for the Northern Yuan. The mark stands on Kunming.

death.label: Zheng He died at sea on the way home, 1433
death.text: Most accounts have him die in 1433 on the way home from the seventh voyage, some say buried at sea. None gives a place, so the skull stands mid-way along that voyage's Calicut–Malacca leg.
death.source: Zheng He (Wikipedia); no source gives the place

alternatives.label: Died at Calicut on the way home, 1433
alternatives.text: On the seventh voyage the fleet called at Calicut on its way back from Hormuz. Some historians have him die there, before it sailed for Malacca.

alternatives.label: Home at Nanjing, died 1435
alternatives.text: A minority view, from later texts and inscriptions, has him live two years more. A tomb is shown at Nanjing.
alternatives.source: Zheng He (Wikipedia); the later Nanjing account

bartolomeu-dias.name: Bartolomeu Dias
bartolomeu-dias.bio: A Portuguese mariner, in February 1488 he became the first European to round the southern tip of Africa, and showed that the way south lies well out to sea, southwest of the African coast. Vasco da Gama used what he found to reach India.

images.author: RedCoat; cut by Biser Todorov
images.note: No likeness survives; a photograph of his statue at South Africa House, London.

death.label: Dias lost in a storm off the Cape, on Cabral's fleet, 1500
death.text: Four of Cabral's ships went down in one storm on the way to the Cape. The wreck's position is not recorded; the skull stands off the Cape.

christopher-columbus.name: Christopher Columbus
christopher-columbus.bio: A Genoese navigator who went to sea young, sailed as far as the British Isles and the Gold Coast, and lived some years in Lisbon. Sponsored by the Catholic Monarchs, he left Palos in August 1492 and made landfall in the Americas on 12 October; he made four Spanish crossings in all.

images.author: Sebastiano del Piombo
images.note: Said to be him; the sitter is not proven, and no authenticated portrait exists.

born.label: Columbus born at Genoa, between Aug and Oct 1451
born.text: Born between 25 August and 31 October 1451 in the Republic of Genoa.
born.doubt: Calvi in Corsica still marks a house as his birthplace, and Catalans, Galicians and Portuguese have each argued he was one of their own.

death.label: Columbus dies at Valladolid
death.text: He died in a rented house, ill, still arguing that the Crown owed him the titles and the tenth of the profits it had promised. He is generally said to have held that he had reached the edge of Asia. His bones were carried to Seville, then Santo Domingo, then Havana, then Seville again, and Seville and Santo Domingo both still claim him.

juan-de-la-cosa.name: Juan de la Cosa
juan-de-la-cosa.bio: Owner and master of the Santa María on the first voyage, pilot on later ones, and maker of the oldest surviving chart to show the Americas, in 1500.

born.label: Juan de la Cosa born at Santoña, c. 1450–1460
born.text: No record of his birth survives; Santoña is the usual account, and the years are read back from his career.

death.label: Juan de la Cosa killed near Turbaco, 1510
death.text: Sailing as pilot to Alonso de Ojeda on the coast of what is now Colombia, he went ashore with a raiding party near Turbaco and was killed by the townspeople's poisoned arrows.

paulo-da-gama.name: Paulo da Gama
paulo-da-gama.bio: Vasco da Gama's elder brother, a son of Estêvão da Gama and Isabel Sodré, he commanded the São Rafael on the first voyage to India. She was burned on the way home, with too few men left to sail her, and he went over to the São Gabriel. He fell ill; his brother took him to Terceira in the Azores and stayed with him until he died. He is buried at Angra do Heroísmo.

images.author: Francisco Pastor Muntó
images.note: A portrait engraving printed in the Diario Illustrado on 30 June 1897, four centuries after his death.

images.author: Álvaro Velho (attributed; Commons credits Vasco da Gama)
images.note: The first page of the Roteiro, the journal of the first voyage, naming Vasco da Gama as captain-major and Paulo da Gama, his brother, as captain of another ship.

images.author: Unknown (Livro de Lisuarte de Abreu)
images.note: A 16th-century drawing of the 1497 armada from Lisuarte de Abreu's book of fleets, with the ships labelled for Paulo da Gama, Vasco da Gama and Nicolau Coelho.

images.author: Concierge.2C
images.note: The left transept of the Igreja de Nossa Senhora da Guia in the Convento de São Francisco, Angra do Heroísmo, with the plaque to Paulo da Gama, who is buried there.

images.author: Anonymous
images.note: A scaled sail plan of the São Gabriel, Vasco da Gama's ship, in a drawing dated 1892; Paulo joined her after his own São Rafael was burned.

death.label: Paulo da Gama died at Angra, Terceira
death.text: Paulo commanded the São Rafael, burned on the East African coast when there were too few men left to sail her. He fell ill on the way home; Vasco left the fleet and took him in a fast caravel to the Azores, and stayed with his brother until he died.

vasco-da-gama.name: Vasco da Gama
vasco-da-gama.bio: A Portuguese nobleman from Sines, in 1497 to 1499 he led the first voyage from Europe to India by sea, round the Cape of Good Hope and, with a pilot taken on at Malindi, across the Indian Ocean to Calicut, the longest ocean voyage made until then. He went back to India as viceroy and died there in 1524.

images.author: Gregório Lopes
images.note: Painted about the year he died.

images.author: unknown master of the Portuguese School

born.label: Vasco da Gama born at Sines, c. 1460s
born.text: Born at Sines, a seaport on the Alentejo coast; some give about 1460, others 1469.

death.label: Vasco da Gama died at Cochin as Viceroy of India
death.text: Sent back to India at last as viceroy, he fell ill within months of landing and died at Cochin on Christmas Eve. His body was taken to Portugal in 1539, and lies today in the Jerónimos Monastery at Lisbon.

ferdinand-magellan.name: Ferdinand Magellan
ferdinand-magellan.bio: A Portuguese officer of minor nobility who served the Crown in Asia, then, refused by King Manuel, took his plan to sail west to the Moluccas to Charles I of Spain. He led the 1519 expedition through the strait that bears his name and across the Pacific, and was killed at Mactan in 1521; Elcano brought the Victoria home in 1522.

images.author: Unknown
images.note: A copy after the portrait in the Naval Museum, Madrid; no authenticated likeness exists.

born.label: Magellan born in northern Portugal, c. 1480
born.text: Born in northern Portugal, possibly around 1480. The mark stands on Sabrosa, where the family house stood.

alternatives.label: Born at Ponte da Barca, by another account
alternatives.text: Wikidata gives Ponte da Barca beside Sabrosa as his birthplace.

death.label: Magellan killed at Mactan
death.text: Magellan took sides in a local quarrel, for Rajah Humabon of Cebu against Lapulapu of Mactan, and went ashore with about fifty men. The ships' guns could not reach the beach, the Mactan fighters came on in waves, and the captain-general was killed in the water. Pigafetta, who was there, called him "our mirror, our light, our comfort and our true guide".

juan-sebastian-elcano.name: Juan Sebastián Elcano
juan-sebastian-elcano.bio: A Basque ship-owner from Getaria, he brought the Victoria home in 1522, the first ship round the world, after choosing to go on west across the Indian Ocean against his orders to return by the Pacific. Charles V gave him arms with a globe and Primus circumdedisti me. Sent out again under Loaísa, he died of scurvy in the Pacific in 1526. Little is known of his private life.

images.author: Unknown
images.note: A Spanish portrait of Elcano painted in the 19th century, three centuries after his death; it hangs in the Museo Naval, Madrid.

images.author: Juan Sebastián Elcano
images.note: The last page of Elcano's will, made in the Pacific on 26 July 1526, days before he died, with the signatures of its witnesses.

images.author: Abraham Ortelius
images.note: Ortelius's 1589 map of the Pacific, the ocean's first printed map, with the Victoria sailing it under the motto Prima ego velivolis ambivi cursibus orbem.

images.author: Artistosteles
images.note: A bronze statue of Elcano in Getaria, the Basque port where he was born.

images.author: Christian Ferrer
images.note: A replica of the Victoria, the Nao Victoria built in 1992, at Sète in France in 2016.

born.label: Elcano born at Getaria, 1486 or 1487
born.text: His own will names Getaria. The year comes from his saying, in August 1519, that he was "approximately" 32.

death.label: Elcano died at sea on the Loaísa expedition, 1526
death.text: He took command when Loaísa died days before, and died himself at sea in early August, in mid-Pacific near the equator; accounts give the 4th, 5th or 6th. No position is recorded, so the skull stands on the equator mid-ocean.

francis-drake.name: Francis Drake
francis-drake.bio: Born in Devon and raised in the Plymouth household of William Hawkins, he sailed on his cousin John Hawkins's slaving voyages and raided the Spanish Main. From 1577 to 1580 he made the second voyage round the world, the first English one, and was knighted aboard the Golden Hind. He was vice admiral against the Armada in 1588.

born.label: Drake born at Tavistock, c. 1540
born.text: Born at Crowndale Farm, Tavistock; the year is reckoned, and accounts differ.

death.label: Drake died off Portobelo, 1596; buried at sea in a lead coffin
death.text: Dysentery killed him on his last raid on the Spanish Caribbean. Drake asked to be dressed in his armour, and was buried at sea in a lead coffin off Portobelo. Divers still look for it.

lapita-people.name: The Lapita people
lapita-people.bio: The makers of dentate-stamped Lapita pottery, who spread from the Bismarck Archipelago through the Solomons, Vanuatu and New Caledonia to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa between about 1500 and 800 BC: the first people anywhere to settle islands beyond sight of land, sailing upwind into the trade winds. No name of theirs survives; the name is the archaeologists', from a site in New Caledonia.

images.author: Patrick Nunn
images.note: A reconstructed head of Mana, a Lapita-era person, in the Fiji Museum; the hair type was guessed.

images.author: Patrick Nunn
images.note: Part of a pot rim from Bourewa in Fiji, dentate-stamped and filled with lime, about 3000 years old.

images.author: Torbenbrinker
images.note: Lapita pottery in the Vanuatu Cultural Centre at Port Vila.

images.author: Patrick Nunn
images.note: Shell rings and cones from the Bourewa Lapita site in Fiji: the people wore shell jewellery.

images.author: Unknown author (plate from Labillardiere)
images.note: A double canoe of New Caledonia, engraved for a French expedition of 1791 to 1794; no Lapita canoe survives, and this is a craft of the same islands.

east-polynesian-voyagers.name: The East Polynesian voyagers
east-polynesian-voyagers.bio: The people who, after nearly two thousand years in West Polynesia, went east in double-hulled canoes to the Cook and Society Islands about 1000–1100 and from there, in some two centuries, to every corner of the Polynesian Triangle: Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa, and on to the Chathams and the subantarctic Auckland Islands. Oral traditions name founding navigators, such as Kupe for Aotearoa and Hotu Matuʻa for Rapa Nui; they are not datable people.

images.author: A. Buchan, S. Parkinson or J. F. Miller
images.note: A sailing canoe of Raiatea in the Society Islands, drawn on Cook's first voyage, 1769.

images.author: Tupaia
images.note: Canoes and a long house on a Tahitian shore, drawn by Tupaia, the navigator-priest of Raiatea who sailed with Cook.

images.author: Sur la route
images.note: The marae of Taputapuatea on Raiatea, the sacred meeting ground from which, in the traditions, voyagers set out for other islands.

images.author: Szilas
images.note: Objects from Wairau Bar in Marlborough, one of the earliest Polynesian settlements in Aotearoa, in Canterbury Museum.

images.author: Phil Uhl
images.note: The double canoe Hōkūleʻa arriving at Honolulu from Tahiti in 1976, a modern voyage made without instruments to show the old crossings could be sailed.

phoenician-mariners-of-necho-ii.name: Phoenician mariners of Necho II
phoenician-mariners-of-necho-ii.bio: Herodotus tells that Necho II of Egypt (610–595 BC) sent out Phoenicians who sailed from the Red Sea round Africa to the Strait of Gibraltar and back to Egypt in three years. Nobody named them.

images.author: SpeakingArch
images.note: A Phoenician war galley under oars on a relief from Nineveh, 705 to 681 BC; the ship was probably built and crewed by Phoenicians in Assyrian service.

images.author: Africa and Its Exploration (wood engraving)
images.note: A wood engraving of 1891 imagines Necho II commissioning the Phoenician crew.

images.author: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg)
images.note: A band of the Balawat gates, an electrotype replica in the British Museum, showing boats of Tyre in the ninth century BC.

images.author: Anonymous (Egypt)
images.note: A relief of Necho II facing the goddess Hathor, made about 600 BC, in the Walters Art Museum.

hanno-the-navigator.name: Hanno the Navigator
hanno-the-navigator.bio: A Carthaginian, sometimes called a king, who sailed down the coast of West Africa in the fifth century BC. Only a Greek periplus tells of it, and nobody agrees how far he went: some say Gabon, others no farther than southern Morocco.

born.label: Hanno of Carthage, 5th century BC
born.text: Nothing is known of his birth. He was a Carthaginian who lived in the fifth century BC, so the mark stands on Carthage.

hatshepsut.name: Hatshepsut
hatshepsut.bio: A pharaoh of Egypt's Eighteenth Dynasty, the eldest daughter of Thutmose I and Ahmose. She began as regent for the young Thutmose III, took the pharaoh's titles by about the seventh year of his reign and ruled with him as senior coregent, c. 1479 to 1458 BC. Her ninth year saw the expedition to Punt, which her temple at Deir el-Bahari commemorates.

images.author: Σταύρος
images.note: Egyptian soldiers of the expedition bearing branches and axes, from the temple at Deir el-Bahari.

nehsi.name: Nehsi
nehsi.bio: An official at Hatshepsut's court, Wearer of the Royal Seal and chief treasurer, who may have been of Nubian descent, going by his name. The Punt reliefs at Deir el-Bahari show him as responsible for dispatching the expedition; some read that as his having led it from beginning to end. He was buried in a rock-cut tomb at Saqqara.

himilco.name: Himilco
himilco.bio: A Carthaginian navigator of the early fifth century BC, sent to explore the Atlantic coast of Europe while Hanno went south. His own account is lost; it survives in brief notices by Pliny and the poet Avienus. Of his family, one scholar makes him Hanno's brother.

pytheas.name: Pytheas
pytheas.bio: A Greek of Massalia who sailed to northern Europe about 325 BC, round much of the British Isles, and was the first on record to describe the midnight sun and polar ice. He gave the world Thule, and first tied the tides to the moon. His own book is lost; he survives in quotation by later writers.

images.author: Mellangoose
images.note: No likeness exists. The page of the oldest manuscript of Strabo (10th century) that quotes him, the text he survives in.

born.label: Pytheas born at Massalia, c. 350 BC
born.text: Known only through later writers who quote him; the year is a reckoning from when he flourished.

nearchus.name: Nearchus
nearchus.bio: A Cretan whose family settled at Amphipolis in Macedonia; one of Alexander's boyhood friends and his navarch. In 326–324 BC he led the fleet from the Indus along the coast and up the Persian Gulf to the mouth of the Tigris.

images.author: André Castaigne
images.note: André Castaigne's painting of the wounded Alexander passing through his fleet on the Indus; an artist's idea of the fleet Nearchus commanded, not a likeness of him.

images.author: ILCNA
images.note: A silver decadrachm struck for Alexander, thought to mark his Indian campaign, during which the fleet Nearchus later led was built.

images.author: Furqanlw
images.note: Eroded badlands at Hingol on the Makran coast of Balochistan, part of the desert shore the fleet followed west from the Indus.

images.author: NASA
images.note: The Strait of Hormuz from the Space Shuttle in 1982, the narrows at the mouth of the Persian Gulf that the fleet passed on its way to the Tigris.

born.label: Nearchus born on Crete, c. 360 BC
born.text: A native of Lato, son of Androtimus, whose family moved to Amphipolis while he was a boy; so he was quite possibly born on Crete.

juan-ponce-de-leon.name: Juan Ponce de León
juan-ponce-de-leon.bio: A Castilian who probably came to the Caribbean on Columbus's second voyage of 1493, he fought the Taíno of Higüey on Hispaniola, then from 1508 took Puerto Rico from its Taíno, put down their revolt of 1511 and was the island's first governor. In 1513 he led three ships north-west through the Bahamas and named La Florida, where the Calusa drove his ships off. He came back in 1521 to settle it, and a Calusa arrow ended the attempt and his life. The fountain of youth was tied to his name only after his death.

death.label: Ponce de León died in Cuba, July 1521
death.text: A Calusa arrow struck his thigh on his 1521 attempt to colonise south-west Florida, and he died in the first week of July, probably of infection, soon after the expedition sailed to Cuba; he was buried in Puerto Rico. No source read names the town, so the mark stands at Havana, the port the expedition made for; the place is a guess.

images.author: Antonio de Herrera
images.note: An engraved portrait of Ponce de León from the 1728 edition of Herrera's history, ringed by figures and a fight with Native Americans; no portrait from life is known.

images.author: Juan Ponce de León
images.note: A 16th-century letter from Ponce de León to Ochoa de Isásaga, with his signature enlarged beside it.

images.author: L. D. Scisco
images.note: Scisco's 1913 reconstruction of the track of Ponce de León's 1513 voyage from Puerto Rico through the Bahamas and round Florida.

images.author: Frederic Gleach
images.note: Ruins at the Caparra archaeological site in Puerto Rico, the settlement he founded in 1508-09.

images.author: Unknown
images.note: A 19th-century engraving of Ponce de León struck down in the fight with the Calusa in July 1521.

juan-garrido.name: Juan Garrido
juan-garrido.bio: Born in West Central Africa about 1480, he went to Portugal as a young man and was in Santo Domingo by 1502–03. He fought in Puerto Rico and Cuba, sailed with Ponce de León to Florida in 1513, one of two free Africans aboard, and went on to Mexico with Cortés. In Mexico City he sowed what he said was the first wheat in New Spain, and in 1538 he asked the Crown for a pension for thirty years of service.

death.label: Juan Garrido died in Mexico City, between 1547 and 1550
death.source: NPS, Juan Garrido: from legal documents
death.text: NPS dates his death between 1547 and 1550 from legal documents; Wikipedia says about 1550, in New Spain. His burial place is unknown.

images.author: Codex Azcatitlan (anonymous Mexica artists)
images.note: A Black soldier in Cortés's company in the Codex Azcatitlan, a sixteenth-century Mexica manuscript; he is often taken for Garrido, but the codex does not name him.

images.author: Diego Durán
images.note: A Black soldier holding a horse in Cortés's party in the Durán codex; some read him as Garrido, others as Juan Cortés.

images.author: Hernán Cortés (Nuremberg edition)
images.note: Tenochtitlan as printed at Nuremberg in 1524 with Cortés's letters, the city Garrido fought in during 1520-21 and later lived in.

images.author: Unknown
images.note: An anonymous seventeenth-century painting of the Noche Triste, the night of 30 June 1520 when the Spaniards fled Tenochtitlan, which Garrido survived.

images.author: L. D. Scisco
images.note: A 1913 reconstruction of Ponce de León's route round Florida in 1513, the voyage on which Garrido is thought to have sailed.

isabel-de-olvera.name: Isabel de Olvera
isabel-de-olvera.bio: A free woman of Querétaro in New Spain, the daughter of Hernando, an African man, and Magdalena, an Indigenous woman. In 1600, before she went north as a servant with Juan Guerra de Resa's expedition to New Mexico, she swore before the town's governor that she was free and unmarried, because as a mulatta she feared someone might annoy her on the journey. The affidavit is nearly all that is known of her.

images.author: Manuel de Arellano
images.note: A portrait of an unnamed woman called a mulata, painted in New Spain in 1711; no likeness of Isabel de Olvera survives.

images.author: Enrico Martínez
images.note: A manuscript map of the provinces of New Mexico and the colony's journeys of 1598-1602, the colony she went north to join; this is a 1906 photograph of the original in Seville.

images.author: George A. Grant
images.note: Juan de Oñate's inscription of 1605 at El Morro, cut by the governor of the colony she travelled to join; photographed in 1934.

images.author: Bureau of Land Management
images.note: A view along El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road from Mexico City to New Mexico that the colonists of 1600 followed.

pedro-alonso-nino.name: Pedro Alonso Niño
pedro-alonso-nino.bio: A pilot from Moguer, near Palos, he sailed with Columbus in 1492, by most accounts as pilot of the Santa María, and again on the later voyages. In 1499 he and Cristóbal Guerra took a small ship to the coast of Venezuela and came home in 1500 with a great load of pearls from Margarita and Cubagua. Accused of keeping back the Crown's share, he was arrested, and died before his trial ended.

images.author: unknown
images.note: A painting of Pedro Alonso Niño seated at a table, held at the Monasterio de La Rábida; its painter and date are not recorded.

images.author: Angle52sales
images.note: A bronze statue of Pedro Alonso Niño at a table in his home town, Moguer, its base reading 'Moguer, América y yo'.

images.author: Editorial Miguel A. Salvatella
images.note: A 1943 map from the Biblioteca Nacional de España of Niño's voyages along the Venezuelan coast, with the 1499 crossing from Sanlúcar and the 1500 return to Galicia as the map labels them.

images.author: Unknown (Drake Manuscript, Histoire naturelle des Indes)
images.note: A Drake Manuscript drawing of a pearling boat off Margarita Island, labelled 'Canau pour pecher les perles', with divers going down with baskets.

images.author: Wilfredor
images.note: The ruins of Nueva Cádiz on Cubagua, the pearl-fishing town later built on one of the islands his 1499 voyage visited.

panfilo-de-narvaez.name: Pánfilo de Narváez
panfilo-de-narvaez.bio: A Castilian who served in the taking of Jamaica and then of Cuba, where in 1513 his men massacred the Taíno at Caonao, as Bartolomé de las Casas, who was with him, recorded. In 1520 the governor of Cuba sent him to Mexico to bring Cortés to heel; Cortés beat him at Cempoala by night, and he lost an eye and was held prisoner. The Crown later granted him La Florida, and in 1527 he sailed from Sanlúcar with six hundred to settle it. In 1528 he marched them inland from Tampa Bay to the land of the Apalachee, who fought them off, and was lost at sea that year; four of the expedition lived.

death.label: Narváez lost at sea, 1528
death.text: He is believed to have been swept out to sea in a storm while the boats worked west along the Gulf coast; nobody recorded where. The skull stands at the middle of the boat leg, and the place is only inferred.

alvar-nunez-cabeza-de-vaca.name: Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca
alvar-nunez-cabeza-de-vaca.bio: From Jerez de la Frontera, he was treasurer of the Narváez expedition and one of its four survivors. Wrecked on the Texas coast in 1528, he lived for years among the Karankawa and other peoples of the coast as a trader and a healer, then walked with Dorantes, Castillo and Esteban to Mexico City in 1536. His account, the Relación, was printed in 1542. Made governor of the Río de la Plata, he marched overland from the coast of Brazil to Asunción in 1541–42, was deposed by the colonists and sent back to Spain in chains, and was tried and sentenced there.

death.label: Cabeza de Vaca died in Spain, on an uncertain date
death.source: Wikipedia, Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca
death.text: His last surviving record is dated 19 May 1559. He died on an uncertain date, at Jerez de la Frontera or at Valladolid.

andres-dorantes-de-carranza.name: Andrés Dorantes de Carranza
andres-dorantes-de-carranza.bio: A captain on the Narváez expedition and one of its four survivors, from Béjar in Castile. Esteban, the enslaved man who walked with them from Texas to Mexico City, was his. In Mexico City in 1536 he sold Esteban to the viceroy; his voyage home to Spain fell through when his ship was found unfit, and he married and stayed in New Spain.

alonso-del-castillo-maldonado.name: Alonso del Castillo Maldonado
alonso-del-castillo-maldonado.bio: A captain on the Narváez expedition from Salamanca, and one of its four survivors. With Cabeza de Vaca and Dorantes he signed the joint report of the journey that Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo copied into his history. He married in New Spain and settled there.

esteban-de-dorantes.name: Esteban de Dorantes
esteban-de-dorantes.bio: Born at Azemmour on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, he was sold into slavery there in 1522 and came to the Americas as Andrés Dorantes's slave. He was one of the four who lived through the Narváez expedition and walked across Texas and northern Mexico, and Cabeza de Vaca says he went ahead and spoke with the peoples they met. Sold to the viceroy, he was sent north in 1539 ahead of Fray Marcos de Niza to look for the cities of Cíbola, and is said to have been killed at the Zuni town of Hawikuh.

death.label: Esteban killed at Hawikuh, May 1539
death.text: Every account of his death here is a Spanish one or a Spanish record of a report; none was written by the Zuni, and the Zuni story comes down through Cushing, a 19th-century ethnographer, as quoted in the National Park Service study. Esteban sent ahead a gourd hung with rattles and two feathers; the chief of the first Zuni town threw it down and said that anyone who came would be killed. He came on, and was lodged outside the town. Fray Marcos had it from a survivor that nothing was given to eat or drink that night, and that next morning, as people came out of the town, he fled, and the wounded survivor saw no more of him. Castañeda, writing years later, has it that he was held three days while the elders questioned him, took him for a spy, found it hard of him to ask for turquoise and women, and killed him, sending about sixty of his followers home. Coronado, 3 August 1540: the death was certain, since things he wore had been found; Coronado wrote that the Zuni said they killed him because the Indians of Chichilticale had called him a bad man who killed and assaulted women. Alarcón, on the Colorado a year later, reporting what the people there told him: the chief asked if he had brothers, and he answered that he had an infinite number, not far off, so the chiefs resolved to kill him. Sancho Dorantes de Carranza: he was shot through with arrows like a Saint Sebastian. The Zuni story as Cushing wrote it down has the Black Mexican killed at Kya-ki-me; another says their wise men kicked him back south. In 2002 Juan Francisco Maura argued that the Zuni helped him fake his death and he lived on among them.
death.doubt: The accounts differ on how and why he died, Zuni tradition puts the killing at Kya-ki-me rather than Hawikuh, and Maura (2002) holds that he was not killed at all.
death.source: Marcos de Niza, Coronado, Castañeda and Alarcón, as translated in Winship; Cushing's Zuni account (Kya-ki-me) as quoted in the National Park Service study, hawikuh-historical-background-study

mansa-musa.name: Mansa Musa
mansa-musa.bio: Mansa, or king, of Mali from about 1312 to about 1337. On his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324–25 he spent three months in Cairo and gave away and spent so much gold that, by al-Umari's report, its price there had not recovered twelve years later. European charts drew him within years: Dulcert's of 1339 names him, and the Catalan Atlas of 1375 sets him on a throne holding up gold. Under him part of the Djinguereber Mosque was built at Timbuktu, and the city grew into a centre of Islamic learning. In Cairo he told a story of how he came to the throne: the mansa before him, he said, had sailed west into the Atlantic with a great fleet and never came back. Siphiwe Baleka of the Balanta Society writes that Mali's wealth came from taxes, trade and enslavement, and that peoples such as the Balanta, who refused its taxes and its rule, remember it as an empire that raided them.

images.note: The king of Mali, labelled Rex Melly, seated on Angelino Dulcert's chart of 1339, drawn fifteen years after the pilgrimage.

born.text: Nobody recorded when or where he was born; c. 1280 is a modern estimate, and the place is given only as the Mali Empire.

death.text: The date is uncertain: estimates run from about 1332 to 1337, and Levtzion thought 1337 the likeliest. Nobody recorded where, so no skull is drawn.

abu-bakr-ii.name: The mansa before Musa
abu-bakr-ii.bio: The king of Mali before Mansa Musa, known only from Musa's own account, told in Cairo in 1324 and written down by al-Umari: he wished to find the far edge of the Atlantic, sent out a fleet of which one ship came back, then sailed himself with a greater one, leaving Musa to rule in his place, and was never seen again. His name is not certain. Al-Umari gives none; Ibn Khaldun, writing decades later, names Musa's predecessor as Muhammad ibn Qu, and the historians who take the voyage seriously mostly attribute it to him; a few suggest instead his father Qu, the mansa before Muhammad. The name Abu Bakr II, by which he is popularly known, comes from a nineteenth-century mistranslation of Ibn Khaldun. No other medieval Arab historian and no West African oral tradition tells of the voyage. Some historians take it seriously; others suspect that Musa deposed his predecessor and told of the voyage to justify his rise.

death.text: No death is recorded. In Musa's telling he sailed west with his fleet and was never seen again; where, or whether he sailed at all, nobody knows, so no skull is drawn.

images.author: Attributed to Abraham Cresques
images.note: The king of Mali on his throne as a Majorcan chartmaker imagined him in 1375, holding up a gold coin; the label names Musa, the man who took the throne Abu Bakr left. No picture of Abu Bakr himself exists.

erik-the-red.name: Erik the Red
erik-the-red.bio: A Norwegian-born chieftain settled in Iceland, outlawed for killings there about 982. He spent his three years of exile finding and naming Greenland, then came back to Iceland and led the first settlers across. He was the father of Leif Erikson.

born.label: Erik the Red born in Norway, c. 950
born.text: The sagas say he came from Jæren, in south-west Norway, and that his father Thorvald fled to Iceland. The mark stands on that district, and the year is a guess.

death.label: Erik the Red died, c. 1003, probably at Brattahlíð
death.text: The saga has him die of an epidemic in Greenland after Leif's return. He was buried in the country he named; the mark stands at his farm.

bjarni-herjolfsson.name: Bjarni Herjólfsson
bjarni-herjolfsson.bio: An Icelandic merchant whose father had gone with Erik to Greenland. Sailing after him in 986 without chart or compass, he was blown off course and became the first European recorded to see the coast of North America, though he never landed. The Saga of the Greenlanders has Leif Erikson buy his ship and follow his sightings.

william-of-rubruck.name: William of Rubruck
william-of-rubruck.bio: A Flemish Franciscan from Rubrouck who had been on Louis IX's crusade. In 1253 he went to the Mongols as a missionary and not, he insisted, as an envoy, across the steppe to Batu on the Volga and on to the court of Mongke at Karakorum. His report to Louis is the best Western account of the Mongols, their customs and the faiths at their court, and Roger Bacon read it.

born.label: William of Rubruck born in Flanders, c. 1215-20
born.text: He is named for Rubrouck, a village in French Flanders. The year is a guess within a decade or two, and sources put it in the 1210s or the 1220s.

death.label: William of Rubruck, last heard of in 1257
death.text: Nothing is known of when or where he died. Roger Bacon, who had talked with him, is the last to mention him, about 1257.

images.author: Unknown
images.note: An illuminated initial from an early 14th-century copy of his Itinerarium: above, William and a companion before Louis IX; below, the two friars on the road.

images.author: Unknown
images.note: Möngke Khan enthroned, in a Persian manuscript of Juvaini's history copied at Shiraz in 1438; William reached his camp in the winter of 1253-54.

benjamin-of-tudela.name: Benjamin of Tudela
benjamin-of-tudela.bio: A Jew of Tudela in Navarre, the son of Jonah; the title of rabbi often given him is not well attested. About 1165 he set out for the Holy Land, perhaps on a pilgrimage and with trade in view, and wrote the Book of Travels, the Sefer ha-Massa'ot, listing the Jewish communities of about three hundred places, their households, leaders and trades, with the days between them. Much of the book is what he saw and much is what he was told.

born.label: Benjamin of Tudela born at Tudela, c. 1130
born.text: He gives Tudela as his native town. The year is worked back from his journey and is a guess.

death.label: Benjamin of Tudela, back in Castile by 1173
death.text: The book says he brought it back to Castile in 1173; nothing is known of his death, and some give 1175.

rabban-bar-sauma.name: Rabban Bar Sauma
rabban-bar-sauma.bio: A Church of the East monk born near Khanbaliq (Beijing), of a Turkic family, Uyghur or Öngüt, who left for Jerusalem with his pupil Markos and was stopped by war in Mongol Persia. Markos became the Patriarch Yahballaha III. In 1287 the Ilkhan Arghun sent Sauma as his ambassador to the pope and the kings of Europe. His account, preserved in a Syriac life of Yahballaha, is the only medieval description of Latin Europe by an East Asian traveller.

born.label: Bar Sauma born near Khanbaliq, c. 1220
born.text: He is said to have been born in or near the Mongol capital, in a Turkic family, Uyghur or Öngüt. The year is a guess worked back from his age at death.

death.label: Bar Sauma died at Baghdad, January 1294
death.text: He returned to the Ilkhanate and died at Baghdad, in the Patriarch's city, aged about seventy-three.

images.author: Arghun
images.note: Part of the Ilkhan Arghun's letter of 1289 to Philip IV of France, in Mongolian script with Chinese seals: the alliance Sauma's embassy had sought.

images.note: A map of Sauma's journeys, from Khanbaliq across Asia to Baghdad and on to Rome, Paris and Gascony.

images.author: HaziiDozen
images.note: Stones carved with crosses from Alimali in the Yuan dynasty: the Church of the East he belonged to lived across Mongol Asia.

images.author: Master of the Mazarine
images.note: The Dominican Ricoldo of Montecroce with clergy of the Church of the East, painted about 1410; Ricoldo preached among them in the Ilkhanate in Sauma's last years.

afanasy-nikitin.name: Afanasy Nikitin
afanasy-nikitin.bio: A merchant of Tver who went down the Volga to trade, was robbed at its mouth and went on rather than go home in debt, through Persia and by sea from Hormuz to India. He spent about three years in the Bahmani country and wrote the Journey beyond the Three Seas, a plain, homesick diary in a mixture of Russian, Persian and Turkic, the first Russian account of India. He reached the Black Sea again in 1474 and is said to have died near Smolensk.

death.label: Nikitin died near Smolensk, 1475
death.text: The Sofia chronicle says it was reported in 1475 that he had died before he reached Smolensk. No source places his death more closely, so the mark stands at the town. Some give the winter of 1472-73.

austronesian-voyagers.name: The Austronesian-speaking voyagers
austronesian-voyagers.bio: Speakers of the ancestral Austronesian language who left Taiwan from about 3000 BC by sea for the Philippines and the islands beyond. Their descendants spoke the languages from Madagascar to Rapa Nui. No name of theirs survives; the name is the linguists'.

marianas-micronesia-settlers.name: The first settlers of the Marianas and Micronesia
marianas-micronesia-settlers.bio: The ancestors of the CHamoru, who crossed from the Philippines about 1500 BC to the Marianas, and the people of Island Melanesia who settled central and eastern Micronesia about 200 BC. No name of theirs survives.

madagascar-austronesian-settlers.name: The Austronesian settlers of Madagascar
madagascar-austronesian-settlers.bio: Speakers of a Borneo language who crossed the Indian Ocean to Madagascar, and became, with African settlers who came to the island, the Malagasy. When they came is argued, from about 400 to about 1000. No name of theirs survives.

james-cook.name: James Cook
james-cook.bio: A Royal Navy officer who commanded three voyages to the Pacific between 1768 and 1779: the Endeavour, which charted New Zealand and the east coast of Australia; the Resolution, which crossed the Antarctic Circle; and the Resolution again, to Hawaiʻi, the Northwest Coast and the Arctic. He was killed at Kaʻawaloa, on Kealakekua Bay, on 14 February 1779, trying to take the ruling chief Kalaniʻōpuʻu hostage over a stolen cutter.

death.label: Cook killed at Kaʻawaloa, Kealakekua Bay
death.text: Cook went ashore to take Kalaniʻōpuʻu hostage until the Discovery's cutter, which Hawaiians had stolen, was returned. He was killed, with four marines (Corporal James Thomas, and Privates Theophilus Hinks, Thomas Fatchett and John Allen); Wikipedia counts 17 Hawaiians killed at Kaʻawaloa. The Hawaiians dismembered his body, partly burned it, and shared the parts among their chiefs, an honour for a high-ranking enemy; three days later more was returned, including his skull, and the crew buried it at sea with full military honours. Whether Hawaiians took him for the god Lono is argued between the anthropologists Marshall Sahlins and Gananath Obeyesekere.
death.doubt: Wikipedia's account counts the Hawaiian dead as 17 at Kaʻawaloa in one place and as 25 round the bay that day in another.

joseph-banks.name: Joseph Banks
joseph-banks.bio: An English naturalist who sailed in the Endeavour with a party that included two Black servants, Thomas Richmond and George Dorlton, who froze to death in Tierra del Fuego in January 1769. In 1774 he introduced the Raʻiatean Mai to British society.

tupaia.name: Tupaia
tupaia.bio: A priest of the ʻarioi at the Taputapuātea marae on Raʻiatea and a star navigator, born about 1725 near Haʻamanino Harbour. In Tahiti he advised the chief Amo and Purea. He sailed with Cook as navigator, interpreter and go-between, drew a chart of the Pacific for him, and was honoured as a tohunga by some Māori in Aotearoa, who gave him a dog-skin cloak. Ten of his watercolours survive. He died at Batavia in 1770.

born.label: Tupaia born on Raʻiatea, c. 1725
born.text: Wikipedia gives Haʻamanino Harbour, Raʻiatea; the mark stands on the island, not on the harbour.

death.label: Tupaia dies at Batavia, 1770
death.text: He died at Batavia, where the Endeavour was docked for repairs, of dysentery or malaria, both of which were aboard. The ship's muster records 20 December 1770.
death.doubt: The journals of Banks and Cook give other dates for his death; Wikipedia treats the muster's as reliable.

taiata.name: Taiata
taiata.bio: Tupaia's young attendant, whom Cook's journal calls "our poor Indian boy Tayeto", Cook's words, not ours. He died at Batavia in early November 1770, some weeks before Tupaia.

death.label: Taiata dies at Batavia, 1770
death.text: Cook's journal records the loss of "his poor Indian boy" on 9 November 1770, at Batavia.
death.doubt: Sources differ on the day; they agree he died before Tupaia, in early November.

thomas-richmond.name: Thomas Richmond
thomas-richmond.bio: One of two Black servants of Joseph Banks aboard the Endeavour, listed in the crew as "a Negro servant" (the crew list's words). He froze to death on 16 January 1769 when Banks's party, collecting plants inland from the Bay of Good Success in Tierra del Fuego, was caught by snow and cold. Banks wrote that Richmond was upon his legs but not able to walk.

death.label: Thomas Richmond frozen to death in Tierra del Fuego
death.text: The crew list records him 'frozen to death' on 16 January 1769. The party had gone inland to collect plants and was delayed by snow; the place on the hills is not recorded.

george-dorlton.name: George Dorlton
george-dorlton.bio: One of two Black servants of Joseph Banks aboard the Endeavour, listed in the crew as "a Negro servant" (the crew list's words). He froze to death on 16 January 1769 when Banks's party, collecting plants inland from the Bay of Good Success in Tierra del Fuego, was caught by snow and cold. One researcher reads the records as showing that Dorlton was Banks's slave, the man called George 'Rupee'.

death.label: George Dorlton frozen to death in Tierra del Fuego
death.text: The crew list records him 'frozen to death' on 16 January 1769. The party had gone inland to collect plants and was delayed by snow; the place on the hills is not recorded.

mai.name: Mai
mai.bio: Born about 1751 on Raʻiatea, he left the Society Islands in 1773 on the Adventure under Tobias Furneaux and reached London in October 1774, where Banks introduced him to society. Reynolds painted him in 1776, and at Kew he took George III's hand and said 'How do, King Tosh!'. He sailed home with Cook's third voyage and was settled on Huahine in a European-style house, with two Māori boys as servants. He died there a few years later.

death.label: Mai dies on Huahine, c. 1780
death.text: Bligh was told, on the Bounty's visit to Tahiti in 1789, that Mai had died a couple of years after Cook left Huahine. Richard Connaughton says the consensus is 1780, probably of natural causes and possibly of an infectious disease.
death.doubt: Wikipedia dates his death c. 1779 in one place and c. 1780 in another, and the cause is not known.

hitihiti.name: Hitihiti
hitihiti.bio: A man of Bora Bora who came aboard the Resolution at Raʻiatea in September 1773 and sailed with her to Tonga, New Zealand, the Antarctic and Easter Island before going home in 1774.

charles-clerke.name: Charles Clerke
charles-clerke.bio: Given command of the Discovery on 26 August 1775, he took over the third expedition when Cook was killed, moving into the Resolution, with Gore in the Discovery. He had caught tuberculosis in a debtors' prison, and died on his thirty-eighth birthday, 22 August 1779, on the passage from the Bering Strait to Kamchatka. He is buried at Petropavlovsk.

death.label: Clerke dies at sea on the way to Kamchatka
death.text: Nobody recorded where. The skull stands at the middle of the leg from the Bering Strait to Petropavlovsk; he was buried at Petropavlovsk, which is the grave and not another place of death.

kalaniopuu.name: Kalaniʻōpuʻu
kalaniopuu.bio: The ruling chief (aliʻi nui) of Hawaiʻi Island. He was at Kaʻawaloa, on Kealakekua Bay, on 14 February 1779, when Cook came ashore to take him hostage until the Discovery's stolen cutter was returned.

te-weherua.name: Te Weherua
te-weherua.bio: A boy of about seventeen from Queen Charlotte Sound who volunteered with Koa to serve Mai, and sailed with Cook to Huahine in 1777. One source says the two boys died of sickness some thirty months after the ships left Huahine.

koa.name: Koa
koa.bio: A boy of about twelve from Queen Charlotte Sound who volunteered with Te Weherua to serve Mai, and sailed with Cook to Huahine in 1777. One source says the two boys died of sickness some thirty months after the ships left Huahine.

marcos-de-niza.name: Marcos de Niza
marcos-de-niza.bio: A Franciscan born at Nice, then in Savoy, who had been with Pizarro in Peru and was a vice-commissary of his order in New Spain. Viceroy Mendoza chose him in 1539 to lead the party that went north to learn of the cities of Cíbola, and Esteban was sent ahead of him. His report, that he had seen Cíbola from a hill and that it looked larger than Mexico City, started the Coronado expedition of 1540, which he guided; Coronado found only Zuni towns, blamed him and sent him back to Mexico. Whether he came near Cíbola at all is still argued.

death.label: Marcos de Niza died, 25 Mar 1558
death.text: One source gives his death as 25 March 1558; the Handbook of Texas says only that it comes from one source. Wikipedia says he died in Mexico; the place is not recorded in the pages read, so no mark is drawn.
death.source: Wikipedia, Marcos de Niza; Handbook of Texas

robert-o-hara-burke.name: Robert O'Hara Burke
robert-o-hara-burke.bio: An Irish-born police officer in Victoria who, with no bushcraft, was chosen in 1860 to lead the Victorian Exploring Expedition from Melbourne to the Gulf of Carpentaria, the first south-to-north crossing of the continent. He reached the Flinders River swamps, turned back, and died at Cooper Creek on the return in 1861.

death.label: Burke dies on Cooper Creek, 1861
death.doubt: The Exploration Committee fixed 28 June 1861 for both Burke and Wills; King's account puts Burke's death a day or two after Wills's, and the place is given as Yaenimemgi in one telling and Burke's Waterhole in another
death.text: Burke died a day or two after Wills, on Cooper Creek near the abandoned depot; King buried him. The mark stands at the depot (the Dig Tree), not the exact spot.

william-john-wills.name: William John Wills
william-john-wills.bio: An English surveyor and astronomer who was second in command and kept the expedition's journal. He went to the Gulf with Burke, and died at Cooper Creek in 1861 of exhaustion and starvation after living on nardoo.

death.label: Wills dies at Breerily Waterhole, 1861
death.doubt: The Exploration Committee fixed 28 June 1861 as the date for both men; Wikipedia gives about 30 June or 1 July
death.text: Wills stayed behind at Breerily Waterhole on Cooper Creek, too weak to walk on, while Burke and King went to look for help. The mark stands at the depot, not the exact spot.

john-king-explorer.name: John King
john-king-explorer.bio: An Irish soldier who joined the expedition as a camel handler, went to the Gulf with Burke and Wills, and was the only one of the four to come back. He was found on 15 September 1861 by Howitt's party, having lived about a month with the Yandruwandha.

dost-mahomet.name: Dost Mahomet
dost-mahomet.bio: A Muslim camel driver from Ghazni, one of the handlers who came with the camels bought in India. He went ahead from Menindee with Burke and stayed at the Cooper Creek depot under Brahe.

roald-amundsen.name: Roald Amundsen
roald-amundsen.bio: A Norwegian polar explorer who changed the plan of his Fram expedition for the North Pole to the South once Peary's claim was news, and reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911 with four men and dogs. He disappeared in 1928 flying north to search for the crew of Nobile's airship.

olav-bjaaland.name: Olav Bjaaland
olav-bjaaland.bio: A Norwegian ski champion from Morgedal and one of the five who reached the South Pole with Amundsen; he was the expedition's ski and sledge maker.

helmer-hanssen.name: Helmer Hanssen
helmer-hanssen.bio: A Norwegian sailor and dog driver, one of the five at the South Pole on 14 December 1911; he had sailed with Amundsen through the Northwest Passage.

sverre-hassel.name: Sverre Hassel
sverre-hassel.bio: A Norwegian sailor and dog driver, one of the five at the South Pole on 14 December 1911.

oscar-wisting.name: Oscar Wisting
oscar-wisting.bio: A Norwegian naval gunner and dog driver, one of the five at the South Pole on 14 December 1911; he stayed with Amundsen on later polar voyages.

silk-road-merchants.name: The merchants of the Silk Road
silk-road-merchants.bio: The caravan traders who carried silk, paper, glass and much else between China and the Mediterranean, most of them over one stretch only, handing goods on from town to town. The Sogdians of Samarkand held the middle of the road for centuries. Few are named; the road was walked by many people and no one is known to have gone its whole length.

ibn-fadlan.name: Ibn Fadlan
ibn-fadlan.bio: A jurist of the Abbasid court at Baghdad who went as secretary and religious adviser with the caliph al-Muqtadir's embassy to the king of the Volga Bulghars in 921-22. His risala, the account of the journey, describes the Oghuz Turks, the Bashkirs and the Rus on the Volga. Nothing is known of his origins, his birth or his death.

giovanni-da-pian-del-carpine.name: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine
giovanni-da-pian-del-carpine.bio: A Franciscan from Umbria, a companion of the disciples of Saint Francis and provincial of Germany, whom Pope Innocent IV chose in 1245 to carry a letter to the Great Khan. With Benedict of Poland he rode to the Mongol court and back, and wrote the earliest important Western account of the Mongols, the Ystoria Mongalorum. He was archbishop of Antivari from 1247 and died on 1 August 1252.

death.label: Carpini died, 1252
death.text: He died on 1 August 1252, archbishop of Antivari. The place is not given in the source read.

nain-singh-rawat.name: Nain Singh Rawat
nain-singh-rawat.bio: One of the first Indian explorers employed by the British to explore the Himalayas and Central Asia, from the Johar valley in Kumaon. He surveyed the trade route through Ladakh to Tibet, fixed the position and height of Lhasa and surveyed a long stretch of the Brahmaputra, and walked 1,580 miles in 3,160,000 counted paces. His reports were first made under the code name Number 9.

quiros.name: Pedro Fernández de Quirós
quiros.bio: A Portuguese navigator in Spanish service who sailed with Mendaña in 1595 and in 1605 led his own expedition from Callao in search of the southern continent. He reached the New Hebrides, took the largest island for Spain as "Austrialia del Espíritu Santo", and founded a short-lived settlement, La Nueva Jerusalén, in Big Bay. He turned back for New Spain, leaving Torres to find his own way.

luis-vaez-de-torres.name: Luis Váez de Torres
luis-vaez-de-torres.bio: Captain of the Almiranta in Quirós's fleet. After Quirós left, he opened his sealed orders, sailed west along the south coast of New Guinea through the strait that now bears his name, and reached Manila in 1607. The passage between New Guinea and Australia stayed little known to Europeans until later in the century.

abel-tasman.name: Abel Tasman
abel-tasman.bio: A Dutch seafarer in the service of the East India Company. In 1642–43 he sailed from Batavia by Mauritius to Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania) and New Zealand, then to Tonga and Fiji, and home by the north coast of New Guinea, without sighting the Australian mainland.

jacob-roggeveen.name: Jacob Roggeveen
jacob-roggeveen.bio: A Dutch lawyer and explorer who, at over sixty, led three ships of the West India Company into the Pacific in 1721–22 to look for Terra Australis. He found Rapa Nui on Easter Sunday 1722, the first European known to have seen it, and sighted islands in the Tuamotus and the Manuʻa group of Samoa. The Arend was lost on a reef in the Tuamotus.

samuel-wallis.name: Samuel Wallis
samuel-wallis.bio: A Royal Navy captain who commanded HMS Dolphin on a voyage of discovery in 1766–68. He was the first European to anchor at Tahiti, where he stayed from June to July 1767 and claimed the island for George III as "King George the Third's Island".

bougainville.name: Louis Antoine de Bougainville
bougainville.bio: A French officer and writer who led the first French circumnavigation, in 1766–69, in the Boudeuse and the Étoile. He reached Tahiti in April 1768, nine months after Wallis, and named it Nouvelle-Cythère. His account of the voyage, with its picture of Tahiti as a gentle paradise, was widely read in Europe.

ahutoru.name: Ahutoru
ahutoru.bio: A Tahitian who went aboard Bougainville's Boudeuse at Tahiti in April 1768 and sailed with her to France, where he spent eleven months in Paris. In 1770 the French shipped him home; he fell ill with smallpox on the way and died in 1771 without reaching Tahiti.

death.label: Ahutoru dies of smallpox on the way home, 1771
death.text: He died of smallpox in Madagascar on the way home, before reaching Tahiti. The mark stands on the south of the island; the place of his death is not given in the sources used here.

william-bligh.name: William Bligh
william-bligh.bio: A Royal Navy officer who had been Cook's sailing master on the third voyage. In 1787 he took HMS Bounty to Tahiti to collect breadfruit plants. After the mutiny of 28 April 1789 he and eighteen loyal men were set adrift in the launch; he navigated some 3,600 nautical miles to Timor in 47 days without losing anyone to the sea.

fletcher-christian.name: Fletcher Christian
fletcher-christian.bio: The master's mate who led the mutiny on the Bounty on 28 April 1789. He took the ship to Tubuai and Tahiti and, with eight mutineers, Tahitian men and women, settled at Pitcairn Island in January 1790, burning the ship. He was killed there in the years after, by most accounts in 1793.

death.label: Fletcher Christian killed on Pitcairn, c. 1793
death.text: The usual account is that he was shot by Polynesian men on the island. The mark stands on Pitcairn, not on the place.
death.doubt: A rumour that he escaped and returned to England has been repeated since 1808; most historians reject it.

john-norton.name: John Norton
john-norton.bio: A quartermaster of the Bounty who stayed loyal to Bligh. When the launch put in at Tofua on 2 May 1789 for supplies, islanders attacked; he was stoned to death on the beach while helping to cast off.

death.label: John Norton killed at Tofua, 1789
death.text: The attack on the shore party at Tofua killed the quartermaster; the rest got away in the launch. The mark stands on the island, not on the cove.

mau-piailug.name: Mau Piailug
mau-piailug.bio: A master navigator of Satawal in the Caroline Islands, trained from childhood in the old way of finding islands by stars, swells and birds. In 1976 he guided the Hōkūleʻa from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti without instruments and later taught the navigation to Hawaiians, among them Nainoa Thompson. He died in 2010.

born.label: Mau Piailug born on Satawal, 1932
born.text: The mark stands on the island.

death.label: Mau Piailug dies on Satawal, 2010
death.text: He died at home on Satawal. The mark stands on the island.
